Problem: Compulsive use and loss of control
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Engagement-optimized ranking, intermittent rewards, endless feeds, autoplay, streaks, and notifications reduce natural stopping cues.
Evidence Snapshot: Problematic—not merely frequent—social-media use shows the clearest association with depression, anxiety, stress, and poor sleep. Restriction studies show mixed outcomes because users may substitute other apps or digital activities.
Most Affected: Adolescents; users with anxiety, depression, loneliness, attention difficulties, or high fear of missing out.
Existing Approaches: Screen-time dashboards, app timers, notification controls, digital detoxes, and parental controls.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: They rely heavily on willpower, can be bypassed, and treat all time equally. Total time does not distinguish meaningful connection from passive or harmful use.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Add a session-intention prompt, finite feed batches, optional hard stops, no autoplay by default, notification bundling, a “Was this session worth it?” check-out, and adaptive breaks based on user experience rather than only raw minutes.
Success Metrics: Unplanned session rate; sessions exceeding intended duration; user-reported control; percentage of sessions rated worthwhile; late-night opens.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Too much friction may reduce legitimate connection or feel paternalistic. Controls must be user-configurable and transparent.

Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Nighttime checking, alerts, emotional arousal, social pressure to respond, and endless content delay bedtime and interrupt sleep.
Evidence Snapshot: Multiple systematic and umbrella reviews find a small but consistent negative relationship between social-media or digital-media use and sleep, with stronger effects for problematic and late-night use.
Most Affected: Teens and young adults; users with irregular schedules, anxiety, or high nighttime notification volume.
Existing Approaches: Do Not Disturb, bedtime modes, blue-light filters, and device curfews.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Blue-light reduction does not address emotional arousal or social obligation. Generic device limits may be ignored or disable important communication.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Create a sleep-aware mode, quiet defaults for minors, scheduled message delivery, a reduced-stimulation nighttime feed, friend-group quiet-hour agreements, and a visible “reply tomorrow” status.
Success Metrics: Opens during sleep window; notification interruptions; self-reported bedtime delay; sleep-window adherence; next-day fatigue pulse.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Emergency or family communication must remain available. Do not infer or diagnose medical sleep conditions.

Problem: Social comparison, body dissatisfaction, and appearance pressure
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Highly visual feeds, edited images, beauty filters, popularity cues, and appearance-focused recommendations distort perceived norms and encourage upward comparison.
Evidence Snapshot: Systematic reviews find strong associations between appearance-related social-media activity and negative body image. Specific behaviors and content exposure predict harm better than total time.
Most Affected: Adolescent girls are frequently highlighted, but harms also affect boys, LGBTQ+ youth, athletes, and users vulnerable to disordered eating.
Existing Approaches: Hidden like counts, media-literacy campaigns, body-positive content, and labels on edited images.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Body-positive content can still keep attention centered on appearance. Labels alone may not undo comparison or repeated exposure.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Hide public counts by default, reduce repetitive appearance-based recommendations, label filters transparently, add a “not about appearance” feed control, audit body representation, and replace public ranking with private appreciation.
Success Metrics: Appearance-content concentration; comparison or distress pulse; public-metric exposure; content diversity; blocks or mutes following appearance content.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Automated systems may misclassify fitness, fashion, health, or identity content. Preserve self-expression and creator agency.

Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Persistent visibility, anonymity, rapid resharing, group dynamics, quote-posting, and low-cost aggression increase the reach and duration of abuse.
Evidence Snapshot: Systematic reviews and longitudinal meta-analyses associate cyberbullying victimization with later mental-health symptoms, although effect sizes and causality vary.
Most Affected: Youth; girls; LGBTQ+ users; racial and religious minorities; disabled users; and public-facing creators.
Existing Approaches: Blocking, reporting, comment filters, keyword controls, automated moderation, and temporary bans.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Reporting usually occurs after harm. Victims must perform much of the safety labor, context is often lost, and coordinated attacks can evade single-post moderation.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Add reply-risk prompts, rate limits during pile-ons, recipient-controlled quote-posting, bystander intervention tools, coordinated-harassment detection, rapid safety mode, and transparent appeal evidence.
Success Metrics: Repeat-offender rate; pile-on velocity; victim response time; harmful-reply exposure; appeal resolution quality; outcomes after safety-mode activation.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Risks include overblocking, language or cultural bias, and weaponized reporting. Severe enforcement decisions should receive human review.

Problem: Harmful-content spirals and vulnerable-user rabbit holes
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Behavioral personalization can repeatedly surface self-harm, disordered-eating, hate, dangerous-challenge, or distressing content after brief engagement.
Evidence Snapshot: Public-health and consensus reports identify harmful-content exposure and algorithmic distortion as meaningful risks while emphasizing that effects differ across users and contexts.
Most Affected: Youth and users already experiencing distress, isolation, eating concerns, or identity-based targeting.
Existing Approaches: Content removal, crisis-resource banners, age gates, keyword intervention pages, and downranking.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Reactive moderation is inconsistent. Binary removal misses borderline content, and crisis banners can become repetitive or easy to dismiss.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Use sensitive-topic circuit breakers, a diversified recovery feed, user-controlled topic cooling, supportive resource handoffs, escalation to trained human review, and no engagement optimization for high-risk categories.
Success Metrics: Consecutive sensitive-topic exposures; recovery-feed acceptance; harmful-content prevalence; recurrence after “show less”; resource engagement.
Risks / Tradeoffs: False positives, privacy concerns, and accidental suppression of recovery communities. Do not diagnose users.

Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Sharing is fast and socially rewarded. Attention is drawn to novelty, identity, and emotion rather than accuracy, and repetition increases familiarity.
Evidence Snapshot: Experiments and meta-analysis show that simple accuracy prompts improve sharing discernment, mainly by reducing intended sharing of false headlines. Community fact-checking can reduce diffusion after notes appear.
Most Affected: All users, especially during elections, crises, health events, and fast-breaking news.
Existing Approaches: Fact-check labels, downranking, account strikes, media literacy, and community notes.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Corrections are often late, labels can become politicized, centralized fact-checking does not scale to every claim, and friction can also suppress true information.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Add context-before-share cards, source provenance, read-before-repost prompts, accuracy prompts for high-velocity claims, community context with viewpoint diversity, uncertainty labels, and citation-friendly posting.
Success Metrics: False-to-true sharing discernment; reshares without opening; time-to-context; correction reach; source diversity; user trust in context notes.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Avoid positioning the platform as a universal arbiter of truth. Distinguish factual claims, opinions, satire, and evolving information.

Problem: Polarization and distorted perceptions of social norms
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Engagement ranking disproportionately rewards moralized, emotional, and intergroup content, making extreme attitudes seem more common than they are.
Evidence Snapshot: Experimental research suggests redesigned feeds can reduce polarizing exposure and improve perceptions of social norms without necessarily reducing enjoyment. Other platform studies show political effects are not uniform.
Most Affected: Civic users, communities discussing politics or identity, and users with little exposure to cross-cutting views.
Existing Approaches: Chronological feeds, downranking inflammatory content, political-content controls, and diverse recommendations.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Forced “both sides” exposure can be unpleasant or legitimize fringe claims. Political balance is difficult to define.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Use representative-not-extreme ranking, source and viewpoint diversity controls, norm-correction cards, separate “understand” and “debate” modes, and remove engagement multipliers for outrage.
Success Metrics: Intergroup or moral-emotional content exposure; perceived norm accuracy; cross-group hostility; source concentration; enjoyment and session-quality measures.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Political neutrality claims require independent auditing. Diversity must not become false equivalence.

Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Platforms collect extensive behavioral, device, location, social-graph, and inferred data to target content and advertising.
Evidence Snapshot: The FTC’s 2024 staff report found broad surveillance practices, weak data minimization, and inadequate safeguards for children and teens among major platforms.
Most Affected: All users, with heightened risks for minors, abuse survivors, activists, and users with sensitive health or identity information.
Existing Approaches: Privacy settings, consent banners, ad controls, account deletion, and youth modes.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Controls are fragmented and difficult to understand. Opt-outs can be incomplete, and inferred information is often invisible.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Use a data-minimal business model, prohibit behavioral ads to minors, perform personalization on-device where possible, provide a plain-language data ledger, allow one-tap recommendation resets, use expiration defaults, and make youth accounts private by default.
Success Metrics: Data fields collected per user; retention duration; percentage of on-device processing; privacy-setting comprehension; deletion completion time.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Strong privacy practices may constrain advertising revenue and recommendation performance. Claims should be technically verified and independently audited.

Problem: Blurred advertising, influencer persuasion, and consumer manipulation
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Native ads, sponsorships, affiliate links, parasocial trust, and personalized targeting blur the line between authentic expression and commercial persuasion.
Evidence Snapshot: FTC guidance warns that children have difficulty distinguishing advertising from content and that disclosures alone may be insufficient, especially for younger users.
Most Affected: Children and teens; financially vulnerable users; followers of lifestyle, beauty, gaming, or health creators.
Existing Approaches: Paid-partnership labels, ad libraries, influencer disclosure rules, and parental controls.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Labels are inconsistent, small, or easy to ignore. Commercial incentives can exist even when a post is not formally classified as paid advertising.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Visually separate ads from social content, use persistent sponsorship labels, provide creator incentive transparency, prohibit microtargeting to minors, explain “Why am I seeing this?”, and offer an ad-free youth experience.
Success Metrics: Ad-recognition accuracy; undisclosed sponsorship reports; youth advertising exposure; ad-dismissal reasons; consumer complaint rates.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Creator monetization may decline. Definitions must cover gifts, affiliate links, sponsorships, and platform-funded boosts.

Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Biased training data, popularity feedback loops, uneven moderation, demographic underrepresentation, and opaque optimization can distort who is seen, recommended, or sanctioned.
Evidence Snapshot: Research documents inequity in ranking systems, stronger bias in online images than text, and asymmetries in recommendation exposure. Mechanisms vary by platform.
Most Affected: Women, racial and ethnic minorities, older users, smaller creators, non-English speakers, and politically underrepresented groups.
Existing Approaches: Fairness testing, representative training data, policy audits, creator appeals, and demographic parity metrics.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Fairness metrics can conflict, demographic information is sensitive, and bias can emerge from both algorithms and the available content pool.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Conduct independent recommender audits, build visibility-parity diagnostics, create multilingual moderation benchmarks, allow users to select ranking goals, reserve exploration space for smaller creators, and improve appeal transparency.
Success Metrics: Recommendation quality by group; exposure inequality; moderation errors by language or group; creator-reach concentration; percentage of audit findings resolved.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Collecting demographic attributes can create privacy risks. Fairness goals must be explicit, transparent, and open to challenge.

Problem: Public metrics, creator pressure, and performative posting
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Visible likes, follower counts, streaks, and virality rankings turn expression into continuous evaluation and encourage content optimized for reaction instead of authenticity.
Evidence Snapshot: Identity research suggests authenticity is associated with clearer self-concept, while idealized self-presentation and comparison can contribute to distress. Direct causal evidence about individual public metrics is still developing.
Most Affected: Adolescents, creators, socially anxious users, and users whose income or status depends on platform performance.
Existing Approaches: Optional hidden like counts, private accounts, close-friends lists, and creator analytics.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Counts may remain visible to creators and continue shaping behavior. Follower totals and algorithmic reach still operate as status signals.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Make reaction counts private by default, use appreciation categories instead of scalar likes, remove streak penalties, provide creator-wellbeing analytics, separate reach from social worth, and encourage authentic posting.
Success Metrics: Posting-anxiety pulse; deletion after low engagement; metric-check frequency; authenticity and self-concept measures; creator burnout.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Creators still need useful performance information. Provide private analytics without turning results into public status rankings.

Problem: Passive consumption, loneliness, and shallow connection
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Scrolling can displace direct interaction while creating an illusion of connection. Outcomes differ between active, supportive use and passive, comparison-heavy use.
Evidence Snapshot: Research increasingly finds that what users do matters more than raw screen time. Interventions teaching connected use can reduce loneliness and fear of missing out, while abstinence may improve other symptoms.
Most Affected: Lonely users, new students, remote communities, users with limited offline support, and marginalized youth.
Existing Approaches: Screen-time reduction, group chats, community recommendations, and wellbeing prompts.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Abstinence can remove meaningful support. Generic “use less” advice ignores beneficial communities and active communication.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Build a connection-first feed, prioritize reciprocal interactions, prompt direct check-ins, distinguish “browse” from “connect” sessions, create community-health indicators, and nudge passive sessions toward conversation or a natural exit.
Success Metrics: Reciprocal interaction rate; meaningful-conversation pulse; passive-to-active use ratio; loneliness or FOMO pulse; follow-up contact after viewing.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Meaningful connection is subjective. Avoid pressuring users to message or exposing private relationship information.

Problem: Unwanted contact, grooming, and exploitation risks
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Open messaging, discoverability, weak age assurance, location leakage, and recommendation systems can connect minors with predatory or coercive adults.
Evidence Snapshot: UNICEF and health authorities identify exploitation, unwanted contact, and abuse as central online-child-safety risks. Prevalence and mechanisms vary across services.
Most Affected: Children and teens; youth in unstable homes; LGBTQ+ youth seeking support; users sharing personal locations or distress.
Existing Approaches: Age gates, restricted direct messages, parental supervision, reporting systems, and known-offender detection.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Age self-declaration is weak, parental controls can reduce privacy or deter vulnerable youth from seeking support, and grooming can develop through many individually ambiguous interactions.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Create an age-appropriate contact graph, restrict adult-to-minor messaging, disable location sharing by default, detect suspicious escalation patterns, offer trusted-contact safety checks, and preserve evidence during reporting.
Success Metrics: Unwanted-contact rate; adult-to-minor DM initiation; response time for severe reports; repeat-contact attempts; youth safety perception.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Age assurance can be invasive. Safety controls must preserve confidential support and avoid unintentionally outing vulnerable youth.

Problem: Opaque feeds and weak user autonomy
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Users cannot see why content is recommended, which signals shaped the feed, or how to meaningfully choose a different ranking objective.
Evidence Snapshot: Consensus reports emphasize platform transparency and user control. Experimental research suggests tailoring recommendations to users’ ideal—not merely revealed—preferences can improve user welfare.
Most Affected: All users, especially youth and people trying to change habits or avoid sensitive topics.
Existing Approaches: Chronological-feed options, “not interested” buttons, topic controls, advertising explanations, and account resets.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Controls are buried, coarse, and slow. Negative feedback may still be interpreted as engagement, and chronological feeds alone do not solve safety or quality problems.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Add a feed-recipe panel, ranking goals such as Calm, Learn, Connect, and Explore, visible ranking explanations, temporary resets, topic-dosage sliders, ideal-preference onboarding, and an exportable feed profile.
Success Metrics: Control discovery and use; feed-goal satisfaction; recurrence of unwanted topics; reset effectiveness; perceived autonomy; explanation comprehension.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Too many controls can overwhelm users. Explanations must be accurate without exposing details that allow manipulation or abuse.

Problem: Moderation opacity, inconsistent enforcement, and low trust
Root Cause / Design Mechanism: Automated moderation lacks context, policies are complex, enforcement differs by language and visibility, and users rarely receive understandable explanations.
Evidence Snapshot: Government and consensus reports warn that AI moderation can be inaccurate, biased, discriminatory, and overly dependent on surveillance. Youth-centered reports call for accountability and meaningful participation.
Most Affected: Marginalized users, non-English speakers, creators, activists, and victims of coordinated reporting.
Existing Approaches: Policy centers, strike systems, appeals, transparency reports, and trusted flaggers.
Why Current Approaches Fall Short: Appeals are slow and generic, transparency reports are highly aggregated, and users cannot see the evidence or rule interpretation applied to their case.
Chrysalis Product Opportunity: Give users a decision receipt showing the relevant rule and evidence, use severity-proportional review, provide fast appeals for account-level actions, test community juries for selected cases, conduct multilingual quality audits, and offer restorative options for lower-level harm.
Success Metrics: Appeal-overturn rate; moderation-decision time; explanation comprehension; error disparities by language; repeat violations after restorative intervention.
Risks / Tradeoffs: Detailed explanations can help bad actors evade moderation. Community review requires privacy and anti-brigading safeguards.
